links.note: 1160 speaks, with irony, of the many who agree to the hard thing, endure the parting and live on afterwards (அரிதாற்றி ... பிரிவாற்றிப் பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்); Parimelazhagar glosses அரிது ஆற்றி as consenting to the parting. 1181 is the woman who did consent (நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன்) and now cannot bear the result. Read together, 1181 shows the cost of the consent that 1160 doubted anyone could really give.

In 1162 she cannot hide the sickness, and telling the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). In 1181 the question widens to யார்க்கு உரைக்கோ, to whom can I tell it at all, because she herself agreed to his going; Parimelazhagar adds that telling a self-made sorrow would itself be blame. The pair traces how the possible hearers for her complaint run out.

1182 has the pallor ride over her body with the pride of saying 'he gave me' (அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால்). 1183 uses the same verb of giving for an exchange: he took her grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor (நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து). The pallor that boasts of being his gift in one verse is entered as his payment in the next.

211 says obligation wants no return, கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு, and points to the rain, which the world cannot repay. 1183 uses the same word bitterly: as கைம்மாறு for the grace and modesty he took, he gave sickness and pallor. The word that names the return a good giver does not ask for is here the name of a bad bargain.

In 1133 the man says he once had shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன்) and today has the palmyra horse. In 1183 the woman says her grace and modesty (சாயலும் நாணும்) are gone and she has sickness and pallor instead. Both lovers reckon love as a loss of நாண் and of a quality proper to their sex, replaced by a public sign of suffering.

In 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits (உள்ளுவன் ... உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and calls it deceit (கள்ளம்) that the pallor comes all the same. In 1250 she tells her heart that by keeping in it the man who left, she will lose still more beauty (இன்னும் இழத்தும் கவின்). 1250 states as cause and effect what 1184 finds baffling: the faithful thinking does not hold the pallor off.

1125 and 1184 open with the same words, உள்ளுவன் மன்யான். The man in 1125 says he would remember her qualities if he ever forgot them, and he does not know forgetting; the woman in 1184 says she thinks of him and yet turns pale. The same claim of constant thought is his proof of love and her complaint that such thought gives no protection.

1185 points there to the lover going and here to the pallor spreading (உவக்காண் ... இவக்காண்); Parimelazhagar takes it as an earlier occasion when he had gone only a short way. 1278 says he left only yesterday and her body has been pale seven days (நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார் ... எழுநாளேம் மேனி பசந்து). One verse measures the pallor's speed in space and the other in time.

In 1277 her bangles understood before she did that the lord of the shore had parted from her (நம்மினும் முன்னம் உணர்ந்த வளை). In 1185 the pallor spreads while he is still in sight. Both make the body register the parting faster than the mind or the facts do; 1277 pushes it to before the event.

1186 is the woman's account: pallor watches for a gap in her husband's embrace (முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும்) as darkness watches for a lamp to fail. 1238 is the man's memory of the same thing: he loosened the arms that held her and her forehead turned pale (முயங்கிய கைகளை ஊக்கப் பசந்தது). The two speakers confirm each other from either side of the embrace.

285 describes those who, with goods in view, watch for another's lapse (பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்), and denies them a loving nature. 1186 gives pallor the same posture: it watches for the weak moment (அற்றம் பார்க்கும்), which Parimelazhagar notes is a figurative use of 'watch'. The book's picture of the thief waiting for inattention is the picture the woman uses for what takes her colour.

In 1187 she lay embracing him, shifted a little (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்), and at once the pallor was thick enough to scoop up. In 1239 the man recalls that a cool breeze cutting between them in the embrace (முயக்கிடைத் தண்வளி போழ) was enough to pale her eyes. Both verses, from the two partners, set the threshold of separation at the smallest physical gap.

1108, spoken in union, calls sweet the embrace that not even air can cut through (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ முயக்கு). 1187 shows what that closeness was guarding against: one slight turn away and the pallor seizes her. The joy of 1108 and the fear of 1187 concern the same unbroken contact.

1188 says people say only 'she has grown pale' and no one says 'he left her' (துறந்தார் அவர் என்பார் இல்). In 1220 the townspeople do say he has left her in waking life (நனவினால் நம்நீத்தார் என்பர்), and she answers that they must not see him in dreams. These are speeches at different moments, but together they show her objecting both when the town blames only her and when it blames him.

1188 complains that the talk fixes on her pallor and not on his leaving. 1190 says it is good to get the name of pallor, provided they do not spread talk of his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்); Parimelazhagar sets it as her reply when the friend has blamed him. The complaint of 1188 should therefore not be read as a wish to have him blamed: in 1190 she accepts the very imbalance she resents.

1181 puts the consent on herself: நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன், I agreed to his absence. 1189 names him as the one who brought her to agree (நயப்பித்தார்) and says let her body pale as it will if he stands well; Parimelazhagar reads நன்னிலையர் as free of fault, while Manakkudavar reads the condition as his suffering too. On Parimelazhagar's reading the two verses share out the responsibility and she keeps the cost.

In 1189, on Parimelazhagar's reading, she accepts the pallor so long as the man who persuaded her is held blameless. In 1236 her arms thin and her bangles slip, and what pains her is hearing him called cruel (அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). In both she ranks his good name above her own wasting.

1190 says being named for her pallor is good if people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்). 1236 says the hurt is in hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து), more than in the slipping bangles. Both verses make the talk against him, and not her own disfigurement, the thing she cannot bear.

1190 hopes that her pallor can be talked of without his நல்காமை being talked of. In 1232 the friend says her pale, weeping eyes themselves seem to tell of the unkindness of the one she desired (நயந்தவர் நல்காமை சொல்லுவ போலும்). The same word நல்காமை shows the limit of her wish: the pallor is itself the report against him.

1191 calls requited love the stoneless fruit of love (காமத்துக் காழில் கனி), fruit with nothing in it to stop the eating; Parimelazhagar explains it as enjoyment without obstruction. 1306 says love without quarrels large and small is like over-ripe and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Both judge love as fruit, and they differ on resistance: the pining woman wants none, while the later verse says a love with no friction is not at its right ripeness.

1108, spoken in union, says the close embrace is sweet to two who desire each other (வீழும் இருவர்க்கு இனிதே). 1191, spoken in separation, says those loved by the ones they love (தாம்வீழ்வார் தம்வீழப் பெற்றவர்) have the stoneless fruit. Both place love's sweetness in the desire being mutual, using the same verb வீழ்; one says it from inside and the other from outside.

1192 says the grace a beloved shows the one who loves (வீழ்வார் அளிக்கும் அளி) is like the sky yielding to those who live by it. 557 says a king's lack of அளி is to living beings what lack of rain is to the earth (துளியின்மை ... அளியின்மை). The same word and the same rain comparison describe the dependence of subjects on a king and of a lover on the beloved.

542 says the world lives looking to the sky and the people live looking to the king's sceptre (வானோக்கி வாழும் ... கோல் நோக்கி வாழும்). 1192 compares the beloved's grace to rain for those who live by it; Parimelazhagar glosses them as those who live looking to it alone. Love is described with the book's standard figure for total dependence on one source.

598 says those without drive never reach the pride of saying 'we are generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னும் செருக்கு). 1193 says the pride of saying 'we shall live' (வாழுநம் என்னும் செருக்கு) suits only those loved by the ones they love. The same construction makes a justified pride depend on a prior condition: inner drive in the one case, being loved in return in the other.

1191 says those loved by the ones they love have 'obtained' (பெற்றவர் பெற்றாரே) love's stoneless fruit; Parimelazhagar ties the word to earlier good deeds. 1194 gives the negative: even those who are esteemed are கெழீஇயிலர் if the one they love does not love them, which Parimelazhagar glosses as lacking good deeds and Manakkudavar as being without what they desire. The pair states the same condition from both sides, and shows the commentators reading it as fortune and not merit.

1195 asks what the one she loves can do for her when he has no love for her (தாம்காதல் கொள்ளாக் கடை). 1245 asks her heart whether a man who does not respond when she draws near (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்) can be dropped as one who hates her (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ). The second speech limits the first: finding no benefit in an unreturned love does not make her able to give it up.

1196 says love on one end only is painful and, like a carrying pole (காப் போல), sweet when on both ends. In 1163 love and shame hang from the two ends of a pole that is her life (உயிர்காவாத் தூங்கும்), in a body that cannot bear them. The same pole carries a balanced, bearable load between two lovers in one verse and two opposed weights inside one person in the other.

118 praises being level like the scale-beam and not leaning to one side (ஒருபால் கோடாமை) as the ornament of the worthy. 1196 applies the same test to love: borne on one end (ஒருதலையான்) it hurts, and on both it is sweet. Evenness between two sides is a mark of justice in the Book of Virtue and a condition of happiness here.

1252 says the thing called desire has no eye, that is no pity (கண்ணின்று), since it works her heart even at midnight. 1197 asks whether Kaman, who stays and acts on one person only, does not see her pain and misery (காணான்கொல்). The complaint moves from the feeling to the god, and both use sight as the test of his mercy.

In 1308 the man asks what use suffering is when there is no lover who knows 'this one is suffering' (அஃதறியும் காதலர் இல்லா வழி). In 1197 the woman asks whether Kaman fails to see her suffering. Both speakers treat pain as needing a witness, and each finds the one who ought to notice absent.

276 ends வஞ்சித்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்: none are harder than those who live by deceiving as false renouncers. 1198 ends with the same formula, உலகத்து வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல், for those who live on without a kind word from the beloved. The phrase that condemns the hypocrite's hardness is turned by the woman on herself, for the hardness of surviving.

1160 says, with irony, that many endure the parting and afterwards stay and live (பின்இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்). 1198 says no one is harder than those who live on without even a kind word from the one they love. Both speeches treat staying alive in separation as something that needs explaining, and neither treats it as a virtue.

1198 calls hard those who live without receiving a sweet word from the beloved (இன்சொல் பெறாஅது). 1199 defines how little would count: though he gives no grace, any report of him is sweet to her ears (அவர்மாட்டு இசையும் இனிய செவிக்கு). Parimelazhagar reads இசை as any word at all, even that he is not coming, and links the two verses on that basis; Kalaignar takes இசை as his praise.

In 1213 her life continues because in dreams she sees the man who gives no grace in waking life (நனவினால் நல்காதவரை). In 1199 the man who gives no grace (நல்கார் எனினும்) still sweetens her ears by any word of him. In both she is sustained by a substitute for his presence, a dream or a report, while saying outright that he withholds himself.

877, in the chapters on enmity, advises: do not lament to those who do not know your pain (நோவற்க நொந்தது அறியார்க்கு). In 1200 the woman tells her heart that it is setting out to tell its great pain to one who is not close to it (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and that filling the sea would be easier. The statecraft maxim and the lover's self-reproach agree that pain told to the unsympathetic is wasted.

In 1237 she asks her heart whether it will win any glory by telling the cruel one, as Pope renders it, of the uproar over her wasting shoulders (பாடு பெறுதியோ நெஞ்சே ... உரைத்து). In 1200 she tells the heart that reporting its pain to one who is not close is harder than filling the sea. Both are addresses to the heart that reject sending him word of her suffering.

1164 says the sea of love exists and the raft to cross it does not (காமக் கடல் ... ஏமப் புணை இல்). 1200 tells the heart to fill up the sea (கடலைச் செறாஅஅய்) instead of telling its pain to the unloving; Pope takes this sea as her own sorrow, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the sea that torments her. On Pope's reading the two verses share the sea as the measure of her grief, with crossing it and filling it both out of reach.
